newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ rates close on new lows after aggressive buying.
newsitem.headline: NZ rates close on new lows after aggressive buying.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.95 (PREV 92.87) 90-DAYS 6.86 (PREV 6.94)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.00 PCT (PREV 6.35) US 5-YR 6.55 (PREV 6.58)
* NZ short rates pushed to new lows by single buyer
* Market shows no inclination to give up gains
* U.S. employment data seen setting tone for Monday
New Zealand short term interest rates finished the week on a healthy note on Friday after being pushed to new lows by a single aggressive buyer.
The 90-days bill rates closed at 6.86 percent from their 6.92 percent open and 6.94 percent close on Thursday. The currency's Trade-Weighted Index was flat at Thursday's closing level of 68.54.

Dealers said a strong buyer had emerged early in the session in the short end and although the market had consolidated slightly once that party had done its dash, it seemed quite content to hold onto its gains.
"One party just came in and hoovered it, both futures and physicals, and then once he'd gone the market just retraced a little bit.
"It's hung onto these levels for most of the day. Sure, we got a push from him (the buyer), but it didn't really back up much from there," an Auckland dealer said.
"It's broken to new lows, so you've got to call that very healthy, and there is nothing to say it stops right here. You would have to favour it being sustainable at this stage."
The session saw impressive volume in the June futures, with 7,454 contracts traded. They ended up 4 basis points at 92.92, helped out by good two-way trading from Australia.
Meanwhile the mid bonds ended six basis points lower in yield at 7.39 percent, while the 11/06s were down three at 7.80 percent.

Dealers said there was good early buying in the short dated bonds. The U.S. Treasury market's rally had given the bonds a firm tone at the open, which was helped by a hangover from comments by Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash late on Thursday. The market read the comments, in an interview with a wire agency, as a sanctioning of easier monetary conditions.
U.S. employment data due tonight NZ time is seen setting the tone for the bonds' open on Monday, followed quickly by local employment figures on Tuesday.
-- Catherine McCaw, Wellington newsroom (64 4) 471 4275
